doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: What makes a music an art form; Charlie Keil and Urban Blues
summary: Mancuso says critics and historians elevate a music, discussing Charlie Keil's Urban Blues, urban versus country blues, and Keil's friendship and move to Buffalo.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: No that’s fine. This art thing. What has to happen for an American popular music style to get to the level of being considered an art form? I mean jazz did. Is blues an art form, and why so?

Well I don’t know what the parameters of how you define an art form, but I think when more and more historian/critics start doing real heavy research and they see there are connections to many other areas, not necessarily Matisse and the French Impressionists movement, because these were mostly uneducated guys and gals doing blues. But the fact that the records were important. Today they call it roots music. I was calling it underground music. But it’s all underground, you know, building up. So I think when the historians and the cultural critics start picking up the momentum of something that they didn’t even know about, a lot of them, or someone like Charlie Keil. When Charlie Keil did his book on urban blues, and you had these other, Samuel Charters and the rest of these guys who really elevated Mississippi — you know, John Hurt and all those older guys — and then those historians put down the city guys because they were unkinking their hair, they were ironing their hair, they were wearing shiny suits and they were playing, and they were plugging those God damned instruments in you know, and they were making a lot of noise, and they were putting that stuff down. And what Keil said, he was a sociologist in Chicago at the time. Anthropology, sociology. And his book, Urban Blues was the key. He said those older guys, you know, unless the performer was broken down and had barely a tooth in his head, was playing not even that well but had made records in the twenties, they were authentic. But Muddy Waters, you know, and Howlin’ Wolf, and these guys in the cities making this loud music as they plugged the things in, they were putting those people down. That’s not folk music. Well it was urban folk continuum. And I remember B.B. King said, “Thank God for Charlie Keil.” And when Charlie did a lot of stuff, he moved to Buffalo, and he wrote my Foreword. And we shared the same birthdate, August 12th. He said we were star-crossed. So every birthday, we started at my house, with martinis and beer, and then we went to his house, for the part II. It was like a caravan. Because he did a lot of playing in music. You know he put together a group with hands-on stuff, and he ran the American Studies program over at U.B. And we actually did the first transfer of us. I went to U.B. to teach those students in his program, American Studies, about the history of what I do now. He came over to Albright Hall and he did the hands-on stuff for the kids, playing all these marimbas and stuff, and shakers. And when he left U.B. he said he had a great point. He said, “I’m tired of fighting the windmills of academe.” And he retired to Connecticut. I shed many a tear when he left. He was one important person. But that whole idea of, when the critics and historians start really paying attention to this stuff, and they see — and the better writers like Peter Guralnick, how they use that imagery of the highways, you know.
